DPI, pixels, and what your form actually needs

Understand DPI versus pixel dimensions so you stop guessing when a form asks for 200 DPI or a size in centimetres.

Pixels are real, DPI is a label

An image file contains a grid of pixels. That grid is the only thing that exists. A photo that is 350 pixels wide and 450 tall contains 157,500 pixels and that number does not change no matter what else you do to the file.

DPI, dots per inch, is a separate number stored alongside the pixels that says how densely they should be printed. Changing it does not add or remove a single pixel. It only changes how large the image comes out on paper.

This is why changing DPI in an editor sometimes appears to do nothing. On screen it genuinely does nothing. It matters when something gets printed, and an admit card is printed.

Converting between the two

The arithmetic is simple. Pixels divided by DPI gives inches. Multiply by 2.54 for centimetres.

So 350 pixels at 300 DPI is 350 divided by 300, which is 1.17 inches, or about 2.96 cm. The same 350 pixels at 200 DPI covers 1.75 inches, or 4.45 cm, because each pixel is being printed larger.

Run it backwards when a form specifies centimetres. A 3.5 by 4.5 cm photograph at 300 DPI needs 3.5 divided by 2.54 times 300, which comes to 413 pixels wide and 531 tall.

When your form gives you both

Some notifications state dimensions in centimetres and a DPI, leaving you to work out the pixels. Others give pixels directly. A few give both, and occasionally they disagree because whoever wrote the notice made an arithmetic slip.

When they conflict, the pixel figure is the one to follow. The upload validator checks pixels, because that is what it can measure reliably. DPI is metadata that many validators do not read at all.

Does DPI affect file size?

Barely. The DPI value is a handful of bytes in the file header. Changing it from 72 to 300 does not meaningfully change the kilobytes, because the pixel data is untouched.

If changing DPI in some tool did change your file size, that tool resampled the image, meaning it actually added or removed pixels. That is a different operation and it does affect quality. Be careful with editors that combine the two settings in one dialog.

What to set

If your notification specifies a DPI, use it. If it says nothing, 300 is a safe default for anything that might be printed, and it is what our resizer uses unless you change it.

The important thing is to get the pixel dimensions exactly right. Get those correct and DPI almost never causes a rejection on its own.
